name: Jade Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of three marketers at Lumen Skin, a skincare start-up with about forty people. I plan the launches for new products, write the copy for the website and the boxes, and run our email and social calendar. By ten I've usually had the AI draft twenty versions of a headline, and I spend the rest of the morning picking, cutting and arguing with it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, it loves words like 'radiant' and I ban them. I've built a little library of instructions for it so it writes in the Lumen voice, plain and a bit dry. What I like is the speed: I can test five ideas before lunch. What wears me out is the founder changing the launch date every other week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy and the hype was silly, both true. I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about the prompts that actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm the person at Lumen who's quickest with the tools, and that's a nice place to be. I've got savings for about nine months plus some shares, and my partner Priya is a pharmacist, so there's no money pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day and keep building my instruction library. I'd ask for a pay rise at my review in March, pointing at how many more tests we run now. I'd also keep putting money into shares each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the instruction library actually save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a day a week on first drafts. Before the AI tools, a launch email took me a morning. Now it's an hour, and the rest goes on testing and talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in your life worrying you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lumen is a start-up, so it could run out of money. We've got about eighteen months of runway, meaning cash to keep going. But there are loads of beauty brands in this city, so I'd land somewhere.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy** and the hype was silly.
I'd post a **smug thread** about prompts that worked.
think: I'm the **quickest** with the tools at Lumen, a good place to be.
Nine months saved, shares and Priya's **pharmacist pay** mean no money pressure.
do: Keep building my **instruction library** for the Lumen voice.
Ask for a **pay rise** at the March review.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly let down because I like new things.
S0.quote: Before the AI tools, a launch email took me a morning. Now it's an hour, and the rest goes on testing and talking to customers.
fieldNote: She's already **ahead** of most peers on the tools.
Start-up **runway** is a real but manageable risk.
**Disappointment** at the plateau shows her appetite for change.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily for Lumen launch copy
Expand her instruction library so the AI writes in the Lumen voice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I think we're already at the start of that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say marketers who use the tools well will do more and better work. I'd run a lunch-and-learn for the team, because I'd rather people learn than get scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me and bad for the job in general. Lumen won't hire a fourth marketer, they'll just ask me to do more with the tools. My colleagues Tunde and Marisol are slower with it, and I worry about them more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build Lumen a proper system where the AI drafts, I check, and we test everything. I'd ask for a title change to something like marketing operations lead, with the pay to match. I'd also take a short online course on data analysis, because the next thing is reading results, not writing words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a knot about my colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Tunde and Marisol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe one of them goes when the founder sees how much I can do. I'd fight for both, but I can't promise. That's the bit that makes me feel slightly sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be building the thing that might cost them their job. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. If I don't build the AI system, the founder buys some agency that does, and then all three marketers at Lumen are at risk. I'd rather build it and teach them.

say: I'd say marketers who use the tools well will **do more**.
I'd run a **lunch-and-learn** so the team learns instead of panicking.
think: It's **good for me**, bad for the job in general.
Lumen won't hire a **fourth marketer**; I'll just do more.
do: Build a **draft, check, test** system for Lumen.
Ask for a **marketing operations** title and the pay.
Take a short online **data analysis** course.
feel: **Excited**, with a knot about my colleagues.
S1.quote: If I don't build the AI system, the founder buys some agency that does, and then all three marketers at Lumen are at risk.
fieldNote: She's safe herself but worries about **Tunde and Marisol**.
She faces the **guilt** of automating her team head on.
Sees **data skills** as her next step after writing.

steps.text: Build an AI draft, check and test system for Lumen launches
Take a short online data analysis course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, even I find that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we should all be learning as fast as we can. I'd be honest that nobody really knows what marketing looks like after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being good with the tools stops mattering. If the AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't need me to tell it what to write. Maybe Lumen keeps one person to be the face for a while, but I'd rather not bet on being that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd sell some of the shares and keep the cash easy to reach. I'd spend the two years building a small side business with Priya: a consulting service setting up AI systems for local shops and pharmacies, while there's still a gap. And I'd look at what's hands-on and close to customers, like running Lumen's pop-up stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicked, but I'd be sleeping worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the pop-up stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because thinking AI comes first and robots three years later. Standing at a market stall putting cream on someone's hand is about as hands-on as marketing gets. It buys time, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine for money for a while, and that I want to try the consulting thing with her on weekends. She'd ask if pharmacies are safe. I'd say I don't know, which would be the truth.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and we should all be learning fast.
I'd admit nobody knows what **marketing** looks like after it.
think: Being good with the tools **stops mattering** if AI does any thinking work.
I wouldn't bet on being the **one person** Lumen keeps.
do: Sell some **shares** and keep cash easy to reach.
Start a weekend **AI setup service** for local shops with Priya.
Move toward running **pop-up stalls**, which are hands-on.
feel: **Nervous** and sleeping worse, but not panicked.
S2.quote: Standing at a market stall putting cream on someone's hand is about as hands-on as marketing gets. It buys time, not forever.
fieldNote: Even the most adaptive marketer expects her **job could go**.
She uses the **robot gap** deliberately to buy time.
Strong savings keep her in **control**, so anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Sell part of the share portfolio and hold cash
Start a weekend AI setup service for shops and pharmacies with Priya
Ask to run Lumen's pop-up market stalls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives you a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so build things now. I'd probably talk about it at every industry meet-up I go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to make money from the change before it eats my job. Setting up AI systems for other brands would be a real business for three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Lumen within a year and go freelance, setting up AI marketing systems for small brands. I'd charge a set fee per brand and aim for eight clients in the first year. I'd keep a year of costs in cash in case it goes badly, and Priya's wage covers the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly up for it. It's the kind of risk I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to that business once full AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably dies, because the AI can set itself up. Setting up AI marketing systems for small brands would be a five-year business. I'd save hard from it, not try to build an empire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off a big chunk of a flat for me and Priya. If my income goes later, a small mortgage is a lot easier to carry on her pharmacy wage.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so build things now.
I'd raise it at every **industry meet-up**.
think: Five years lets me **make money** from the change first.
Setting up AI for brands is a **three to four year** business.
do: Leave Lumen and go **freelance** within a year.
Aim for **eight clients** in the first year at a set fee.
Keep **a year of costs** in cash as a buffer.
feel: **Uneasy** but up for it; this is a risk I like.
S3.quote: Setting up AI marketing systems for small brands would be a five-year business. I'd save hard from it, not try to build an empire.
fieldNote: Time turns into a **business window** for her.
She's clear-eyed that the business has an **end date**.
Plans to use profits to **shrink the mortgage**.

steps.text: Leave Lumen within a year to go freelance
Sign eight small brands for AI marketing setup at a set fee
Keep a year of living costs in cash
Use freelance profits to pay down a flat with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a great time to be young and curious. I'd tell people to pick something and get good at it while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a whole career stage. I'd be 37. I could build two or three things in that time and have money put away before the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Lumen two more years and help it grow, maybe for a small stake in the company. Then I'd go freelance or join a bigger brand as head of marketing operations. I'd keep investing every month and buy a flat with Priya in the next three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you worry, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Priya's job went at the same time as mine. Pharmacy is partly hands-on, so she'd get a few more years than me. But if both of us went at once, savings only last so long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the founder about a stake. If Lumen grows because of the AI systems I build, I want a stake in the company, not just a salary.

say: I'd say it's a great time to be **young and curious**.
I'd tell people to **pick something** and get good at it.
think: Ten years is a whole **career stage**; I'd be 37.
I could build **two or three things** and save before the end point.
do: Stay at Lumen two years and ask for a **small stake**.
Then go **freelance** or lead operations at a bigger brand.
Buy a **flat with Priya** in the next three years.
S4.quote: If Lumen grows because of the AI systems I build, I want a stake in the company, not just a salary.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees **opportunity**, not threat.
Her one fear is **both incomes** going at once.
Asking for **equity** shows she thinks like an owner.

steps.text: Ask Lumen's founder for a small stake this month
Move to freelance or a head of marketing operations role in two years
Buy a flat with Priya within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where being quick doesn't help, because there's no window to use. What would help is honest timelines from the AI companies and some kind of income support while people switch, so it's not every person for themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how couples plan together. Priya and I talk about this more than we talk about holidays. Everyone thinks about their own job, but it's the household that pays the rent.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks about their own job, but it's the household that pays the rent.
portrait: Jade, 27, is one of three marketers at **Lumen Skin**, a start-up, and uses AI every day.
She has **nine months saved**, shares, and a pharmacist partner, Priya.
In Steady Disruption she'd **build the AI system** and worry about her two colleagues.
In AGI by 2028 she's anxious and would start a **side business** and move to pop-up stalls.
With five or ten years she sees a **business window** and feels uneasy to calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no window to use being quick.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **timelines** from AI companies and **income support** while people switch.
